nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Decide how a small SaaS replaces Google Analytics with a self-hosted, privacy-friendly setup
nodes.body:
## Destination
A one-page decision record. It states which tool we use, where it runs, what we track, how we migrate, and what it costs per month.

## Notes
- **SaaS**: our B2B web app (app.example.com) plus our marketing site (www.example.com).
- **Product analytics**: in-app events, such as signup and feature use. This is different from marketing page views.
- **Marketing analytics**: page views, referrers and campaigns on the marketing site.
- Standing preferences: low ops burden. EU customers matter. Avoid cookie banners if possible.

## Done when
- The tool is chosen.
- The hosting is chosen.
- The event list is agreed.
- The migration steps are written.
- The monthly cost is estimated.
- The GDPR stance is stated.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Do we use one tool for both sites, or one tool for each?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** Today Google Analytics (GA) covers the marketing site and maybe the app. We want to replace it with a self-hosted, privacy-friendly setup.

**The problem:** The two sites need different things. The marketing site needs page views, referrers and campaigns. The app needs events per user, such as signup and feature use, and funnels. Some tools do both. Some tools do only one job well.

**What hangs on it:** The tool choice, the hosting, the cost, and the ops burden. Two tools double the work to run them.

options.label: One tool for both sites (recommended)
options.detail: One install covers page views on www and events in the app. Cost: the tool must be good at both jobs, so fewer tools qualify.

options.label: Two tools, one per job
options.detail: A light page-view tool runs on www. A product analytics tool runs in the app. Cost: two installs to run, two bills, and two places to look.

options.label: Product analytics only
options.detail: We track the app well and keep only simple counts on www, for example from server logs. Cost: we lose campaign and referrer reports for marketing.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Who runs the analytics servers?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** The goal says "self-hosted". The standing preferences also say low ops burden and EU customers matter.

**The problem:** These pull in different directions. Running the tool ourselves gives full control of the data. It also adds upgrades, backups and monitoring. Many open-source tools also sell a managed cloud in the EU. That keeps the data in the EU with little ops work, but the vendor holds the data.

**What hangs on it:** The monthly cost, the ops tasks we must plan, and part of the GDPR stance.

options.label: The tool vendor runs it in the EU (recommended)
options.detail: We use the managed cloud of an open-source tool, with an EU data region. Cost: a monthly fee, and the data is on the vendor's servers, not ours.

options.label: We run it on a small EU server
options.detail: We install the open-source tool on one rented server in the EU. Cost: we do upgrades, backups and monitoring ourselves.

options.label: We run it on our existing app infrastructure
options.detail: The tool runs next to the app, in our current cloud account. Cost: analytics load can affect the app, and the same team carries it.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: In the app, do we track named users or only anonymous counts?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** We want to avoid cookie banners. We also want product analytics in the app, such as signup and feature use.

**The problem:** Anonymous page counts without cookies usually need no banner. Linking events to a logged-in user is personal data. It needs a legal basis, for example our contract with the customer or legitimate interest. Example: "account Acme used the export feature 12 times this week" is personal data. "The export feature was used 340 times" is not.

**What hangs on it:** Which tools qualify, the event list, whether we need a banner, and the GDPR stance.

options.label: Named users in the app, anonymous on www (recommended)
options.detail: The app links events to the logged-in account. The marketing site uses no cookies and no personal data. Cost: the app privacy notice must cover analytics, and the tool must store user ids.

options.label: Anonymous everywhere
options.detail: No user ids on either site. No banner anywhere. Cost: no per-user or per-account funnels, so questions such as 'which accounts use feature X' stay open.

options.label: Named users everywhere, with a banner
options.detail: Both sites set cookies and link visits to people. Cost: a cookie banner on www, which we want to avoid, and less data from people who decline.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What do we do with our historical Google Analytics data?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** We will remove Google Analytics (GA). GA holds our past traffic data.

**The problem:** The new tool counts differently. Most old data cannot move over cleanly. We must decide what, if anything, we keep.

**What hangs on it:** The migration steps, and whether we run GA and the new tool side by side for a while.

options.label: Export key reports, then drop GA (recommended)
options.detail: We save a few monthly summaries, such as visits per page and per source, as files. Cost: we cannot query the old raw data later.

options.label: Import history into the new tool
options.detail: We load old GA data into the new tool, so charts run back in time. Cost: few tools support this well, and the numbers do not match one to one.

options.label: Start fresh, keep nothing
options.detail: We remove GA and start from zero. Cost: no year-over-year comparison for the first year.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: List what we use Google Analytics for today
nodes.body:
Write down every report, dashboard, alert and integration that uses Google Analytics (GA) today, and who uses it. Include links to Google Ads or other tools, for example conversion tracking.

This tells us what the new setup must replace, and what we can drop. The tool choice and the migration steps depend on it.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Measure our monthly traffic and event volume
nodes.body:
Find the numbers for one normal month:
- page views on the marketing site
- page views and active users in the app
- an estimate of in-app events, for example signups and feature use

Most analytics tools price by monthly events or page views. Server size also depends on volume. The monthly cost estimate cannot start without these numbers.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Draft the first event list for the app
nodes.body:
Write a short list of in-app events, for example: signed up, invited a teammate, created first project, used feature X, upgraded plan. For each event, write the question it answers and the properties it carries.

Keep it small: 10 to 20 events. Mark any property that is personal data. The answer to "In the app, do we track named users or only anonymous counts?" decides which properties are allowed.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Candidate tools fall into two groups
nodes.body:
This is my inference from general knowledge, not yet checked against current vendor pages.

- **Page-view tools**: Plausible, Umami, Matomo. They count visits without cookies. They are light to run. Matomo also has some event and user features.
- **Product analytics tools**: PostHog. It tracks events per user, funnels and retention. It is much heavier to self-host.

Plausible, Umami, Matomo and PostHog all have an open-source version and a managed cloud. Check the prices and EU regions before a choice.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What GDPR documents and steps do we need?
nodes.body: The GDPR stance must be stated. The exact parts are not clear yet. Likely areas: a data processing agreement with any vendor, the privacy notice text, how long we keep data, and how we handle a request to delete a user's data. The answers to the hosting and named-user questions shape this.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What breaks when ad blockers block the tracker?
nodes.body: Many ad blockers block analytics scripts, also privacy-friendly ones. Our numbers could be low, mostly among technical B2B users. Options may include a proxy on our own domain, or sending app events from the server. The size of the problem and the fix are not clear yet.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: How do we run the cut-over from Google Analytics?
nodes.body: The migration order is not clear yet. Open points: do we run both tools side by side, for how long, how we check that the numbers agree, and when we remove the GA script and any cookie banner.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Who reads the analytics, and in what form?
nodes.body: We do not know yet who looks at the numbers: founders, marketing, product, sales. Each group may need different views, such as a weekly email, a shared dashboard, or account data in the CRM. This may add needs to the tool choice.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Named users in the app, anonymous on www (recommended)
nodes.body: Yes. Customers already sign a DPA with us, analytics in the app goes under that. Marketing site stays anonymous, no banner. I hate cookie banners.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: We run it ourselves on Hetzner (Germany), Docker Compose, same as everything else. No Kubernetes. Our DevOps contractor has ~10h/month, so it has to be boring to run.
nodes.body: Not against an EU cloud plan if it's clearly cheaper than his hours. Budget is ~80 EUR/month max. We already run Postgres there, if the tool can use it, even better.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Export key reports, then drop GA (recommended)
nodes.body: Jonas (marketing) wants the last 12 months of monthly totals. Nobody needs raw data.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Ballpark: 40k pageviews, ~2M app events/month
nodes.body:
Rough numbers:
- marketing site: ~40k pageviews/month
- app: ~1,800 weekly active users
- if we track features properly, maybe 2M events/month. That is a guess.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: GA today: page views, UTM campaigns, signup hack
nodes.body:
Honestly not much:
- marketing page views + UTM campaign tracking. Jonas cares about this one.
- a few hacked signup "events".
Nobody looks at the GA funnels. No Google Ads conversion stuff I know of, will ask Jonas.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: App events link to the logged-in account; www stays anonymous with no cookies
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user** in reply to "In the app, do we track named users or only anonymous counts?".

- **App (app.example.com):** events link to the logged-in user and account. The legal basis is the data processing agreement (DPA) that each customer already signs with us. Analytics in the app goes under that DPA.
- **Marketing site (www.example.com):** anonymous counts only. No cookies, no personal data, no cookie banner.

What follows from this (my inference):
- The tool must support an "identify" call for the app, and a cookieless mode for www.
- If a vendor cloud stores app events, that vendor becomes a sub-processor. Our customer DPA must then list it.
- "Draft the first event list for the app" can now start: user id and account id are allowed properties in the app.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: We self-host on Hetzner in Germany with Docker Compose, for 80 EUR/month or less
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user** in reply to "Who runs the analytics servers?".

- **Where:** our own Hetzner servers in Germany, next to what we already run.
- **How:** Docker Compose. No Kubernetes.
- **Ops budget:** our DevOps contractor has about 10 hours per month in total. The tool must be boring to run: few moving parts, easy upgrades.
- **Money budget:** 80 EUR per month at most.
- **Exception:** an EU managed cloud is allowed if it is clearly cheaper than the contractor's hours.
- **Bonus:** we already run Postgres there. A tool that can use it is preferred.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Keep 12 months of monthly totals as files, then remove Google Analytics
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user** in reply to "What do we do with our historical Google Analytics data?".

- Jonas (marketing) gets the last 12 months of monthly totals, exported from Google Analytics (GA) as files.
- Nobody needs the raw data. We do not import history into the new tool.
- After the export, we remove GA.

So GA import support does not count when we compare tools.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Planning volume: about 40k page views and 2M app events per month
nodes.body:
Source: the user's estimate in "Ballpark: 40k pageviews, ~2M app events/month". The app event number is a guess.

| Site | Volume per month |
|---|---|
| www.example.com | about 40,000 page views |
| app.example.com | about 1,800 weekly active users, about 2,000,000 events |

What this means (my inference, prices from "Tool facts checked against vendor pages"):
- 40k page views is small. Every candidate tool handles it, and some free cloud tiers cover it.
- 2M events is about 1,100 events per active user per month, or about 50 per user per working day. That is a lot for a first event list of 10 to 20 events. The real number is likely lower.
- The app number decides the cost. It also rules out PostHog self-hosted, which its vendor says struggles above about 300k events per month.
- We can use these numbers for the cost estimate now. We check them after one month on the new tool.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: The new setup must replace page views, UTM campaigns and signup events
nodes.body:
Source: the user's list in "GA today: page views, UTM campaigns, signup hack".

**Must replace:**
- Page views on the marketing site.
- UTM campaign tracking. A UTM tag is a set of parameters in a link, such as `?utm_source=newsletter`, that says where a visitor came from. Jonas (marketing) uses this.
- Signup events. Today these are hacked into GA. In the new setup they become real events in "Draft the first event list for the app".

**Can drop:** GA funnels. Nobody looks at them.

**Not known yet:** Google Ads conversion tracking. The user will ask Jonas. If Google Ads needs conversions, we need a plan for it, because the Ads tag sets its own cookies.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Ask Jonas about Google Ads and the 12 monthly totals he wants
nodes.body:
Before we remove Google Analytics (GA), ask Jonas (marketing) two things:

1. **Google Ads:** do we send conversions from GA to Google Ads, or run any Ads campaign that depends on GA? If yes, removing GA breaks it.
2. **Monthly totals:** which totals does he want for the last 12 months? For example: page views per page, visits per source, visits per UTM campaign, signups per month.

Write his answers as an answer to this task. Answer 1 can change the tool choice. Answer 2 sets the export step in the cut-over.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What the four candidate tools need and do, from their own pages
nodes.body:
**Why this node exists:** "Candidate tools fall into two groups" named four tools: Umami, Plausible, Matomo and PostHog. This node checks each one against the vendor's own pages. It tests them against our limits: Hetzner, Docker Compose, 80 EUR/month or less, and a contractor with about 10 hours per month.

**Terms used below:**
- *Identify*: link events to the logged-in account.
- *Funnel*: the share of users who go through steps in order, for example signup, then first project.
- *Retention*: the share of users who come back in later weeks.
- *ClickHouse*: a second database type that some tools need. It is one more service to run and back up.

**Umami**
- To run it: one container and a Postgres database. Docker Compose works.
- www without cookies: yes.
- App: identify, funnels and retention, all three.
- Cloud price: free up to 100k events/month for 1 site; Pro is $20/month.

**Plausible Community Edition (self-hosted)**
- To run it: Postgres plus ClickHouse, Docker Compose, 2 GB RAM.
- www without cookies: yes.
- App: custom events only. No identify, no retention, no funnels in the self-hosted edition.
- Cloud price: $19 to $39/month at 100k page views. No free tier.

**Matomo**
- To run it: PHP and MySQL or MariaDB. It does not support Postgres.
- www without cookies: possible. But Matomo says that in Germany, only its server-log mode is clearly free of consent.
- App: User ID, yes. Funnels: the pages did not say; it may be a paid plugin.
- Cloud price: Frankfurt hosting, €29/month for 50k hits.

**PostHog**
- To run it: Postgres, ClickHouse, Kafka, Redis, Zookeeper and MinIO, on 4 vCPU and 16 GB. The vendor gives no support for this. It warns it may struggle above about 300k events/month.
- www without cookies: yes, in its cookieless mode.
- App: identify, funnels and retention. Its reports are the deepest of the four.
- Cloud price: Frankfurt hosting. The first 1M events per month are free, then about $0.00005 per event. At 2M events that is about $50/month. Identified events can cost more.

**What this changes:**
- Umami is more than a page-view counter. It covers the app too.
- PostHog self-hosted does not fit our ops budget. Only its cloud is a real option.
- Matomo adds a MySQL database next to our Postgres.

**Hosting cost:** a Hetzner 4 vCPU / 8 GB shared server (CX33) is about €8.99/month. The page showed some plans as "currently unavailable", so check before you order.

All prices exclude VAT. Checked on 2026-11-17.

Sources:
- https://docs.umami.is/docs/install, https://docs.umami.is/docs, https://umami.is/pricing
- https://github.com/plausible/community-edition, https://plausible.io/self-hosted-web-analytics, https://plausible.io/
- https://matomo.org/faq/on-premise/matomo-requirements/, https://matomo.org/faq/new-to-piwik/how-do-i-use-matomo-analytics-without-consent-or-cookie-banner/, https://matomo.org/pricing/
- https://posthog.com/docs/self-host, https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/js/persistence.md, https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/pricing
- https://www.hetzner.com/cloud/cost-optimized

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Which tool do we run for the app and the marketing site?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** We self-host on Hetzner with Docker Compose, for 80 EUR/month or less, and the contractor has about 10 hours per month. The app tracks named users; www stays anonymous with no cookies. "Tool facts checked against vendor pages" lists what each tool needs.

**The problem:** No tool is best at every part. Umami fits the hosting best: it uses our Postgres and does both jobs. PostHog has the deepest product analytics, but only its cloud fits our ops budget. Matomo is left out: it cannot use Postgres and adds MySQL. PostHog self-hosted is left out: it needs six services and struggles at our volume.

**What hangs on it:** This answer also settles "Do we use one tool for both sites, or one tool for each?". It sets the monthly cost, the sub-processor list in our DPA, how events are sent, and the cut-over steps.

options.label: Umami for both, on our Postgres (recommended)
options.detail: One small container on our Hetzner server, using the Postgres we already run. Cookieless on www, identify, funnels and retention in the app. Cost: near zero money. Risk: about 2M events/month add load to our shared Postgres, and its reports are simpler than PostHog's.

options.label: Umami on www, PostHog EU cloud for the app
options.detail: Umami counts www as above. PostHog in Frankfurt does the app. Cost: about $50/month at 2M events, two tools to learn, and PostHog becomes a sub-processor in our customer DPA.

options.label: PostHog EU cloud for both
options.detail: One tool, nothing to run. www uses PostHog's cookieless mode. Cost: about $50/month or more, close to the 80 EUR budget, and all data sits with the vendor.

options.label: Plausible self-hosted on www, Umami in the app
options.detail: Plausible has the most polished marketing reports. Cost: two tools, and Plausible adds a ClickHouse database for the contractor to run.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: How long do Google Analytics and the new tool run side by side?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** We keep 12 months of monthly totals as files, then remove Google Analytics (GA).

**The problem:** The new tool will count fewer visits than GA. Cookieless tools count visitors in a different way, and ad blockers block some scripts. If we switch on one day, nobody can tell a real drop from a counting change. Example: GA shows 40,000 page views in a month; the new tool shows 33,000 for the same month. With an overlap, we know the 18% gap is the tool, not lost traffic.

**What hangs on it:** The order of the cut-over steps, the date of Jonas's export, and the date we remove the GA script.

options.label: One month side by side, then remove GA (recommended)
options.detail: Both tools count the same month. We compare page views and signups, then Jonas exports his totals and we remove GA. Cost: one more month of the GA script on our sites.

options.label: No overlap: export, then switch the same day
options.detail: Jonas exports his totals, we remove GA and add the new tool at once. Cost: we cannot tell whether a change in numbers is real or comes from the new tool.

options.label: Three months side by side
options.detail: A longer comparison, which also covers a full campaign cycle for Jonas. Cost: three months of two tools and of the GA script.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Umami for both, on our Postgres (recommended)
nodes.body: Umami for both, fine. But I don't want 2M events/month hitting our main app DB — put Umami on its own Postgres database (separate instance if needed). If it gets slow we revisit PostHog cloud.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Session replay — worth it, or a privacy problem?
nodes.body: Curious about session replay for the app — seeing where architects get stuck would help. But I worry about privacy: our customers' project data is on screen. Does any of these do it with masking? Not a must-have.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Jonas: Ads uses GA4 signup conversions; fine with another upload path
nodes.body: Talked to Jonas. He runs small Google Ads campaigns, ~€1.5k/month, and imports signup conversions from GA4 into Ads. So removing GA breaks that. He's OK uploading conversions another way (offline conversion import or server-side) as long as it's not much work. For the 12 months: monthly totals is enough for him.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Umami runs both sites, on its own Postgres, apart from the app database
nodes.body:
**What is settled:** One tool, Umami, counts page views on www and events in the app. This also answers "Do we use one tool for both sites, or one tool for each?": one tool.

**The change from the recommended option:** Umami does not use the app's main Postgres. It gets its own Postgres database, on a separate instance if needed. About 2M app events per month must not load the app database.

**What this means in practice** (our inference, not a vendor statement):
- Docker Compose runs two services: the Umami container and its own Postgres container. Umami reads the database address from one setting (`DATABASE_URL`), so this costs no extra work in Umami.
- The new Postgres needs its own backup. The contractor adds it to the backup job he runs today.
- It can share the Hetzner server at first. If load grows, it moves to its own server, for about €9/month.

**When we revisit:** if Umami gets slow, we look again at PostHog EU cloud for the app (about $50/month at 2M events).

Source: https://docs.umami.is/docs/install

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Umami and PostHog both record sessions and can hide all text on screen
nodes.body:
**Your question:** can any candidate tool record app sessions (session replay) and hide our customers' project data?

**Short answer:** yes. Umami, our chosen tool, can do it on our own server. So the recordings never leave Hetzner.

**Umami** (since version 3.1.0, self-hosted too):
- You switch it on per website, in the admin page "Replays & Heatmaps". A second small script loads next to the tracker.
- Default mode hides all input fields. A strict mode hides all inputs and all text on the page. You can also hide chosen page parts with CSS selectors.
- It records 15% of sessions by default; you can set 0% to 100%.
- A recording stops after 5 minutes by default. Umami keeps recordings for 30 days; you can save the ones you want.

**PostHog** (cloud only for us, see "Umami runs both sites, on its own Postgres, apart from the app database"):
- It hides input fields by default, but not other text.
- To hide all text, set `maskTextSelector: "*"`. To blank a whole area, add the class `ph-no-capture`.

**Plausible:** no session replay. **Matomo:** only through a paid plugin; not checked further, because Matomo is out.

**Risks, our inference:**
- Strict mode hides text, but it does not hide images, canvas drawings or plans. Architects' drawings may still show. Test on a real project screen before you switch it on.
- Recordings tie to named users in the app. Our privacy notice and customer contract must then say we record sessions.
- Recordings add data to the Umami Postgres. A low sample rate keeps this small.

**If you want it later:** strict mode, a low sample rate (for example 5%), and a test on real screens first. It needs no new tool.

Sources:
- https://docs.umami.is/docs, https://docs.umami.is/docs/replays
- https://posthog.com/docs/session-replay/privacy

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Jonas needs monthly totals only, and a new path for Google Ads signup conversions
nodes.body:
**What Jonas told us** (recorded in "Jonas: Ads uses GA4 signup conversions; fine with another upload path"):

1. **Google Ads:** He spends about €1.5k/month on small Google Ads campaigns. Today Google Ads imports signup conversions from Google Analytics (GA4). When we remove GA, this import stops.
2. **Path:** he accepts another way to send signups to Google Ads, if it is little work.
3. **History:** monthly totals for the last 12 months are enough for him.

**What this settles:**
- The export step in "Keep 12 months of monthly totals as files, then remove Google Analytics" is monthly totals only. No daily data.
- We do not remove GA before the new path for Ads conversions works. Otherwise his campaigns run blind.

**What it opens:** "How do we send signup conversions to Google Ads without Google Analytics?"

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Google Ads takes signups from our server if we keep the ad click id
nodes.body:
**Why this matters:** Jonas's Google Ads campaigns need signup conversions. Today they come from Google Analytics, which we remove.

**How Google Ads takes conversions without its script** (Google's "offline conversion import"):
- Google adds a click id, `gclid`, to the landing page address when someone clicks an ad. This needs auto-tagging on in the Ads account.
- We keep that id with the new account. Later we upload rows of "click id, conversion name, time".
- Upload ways: Google Sheets with a scheduled import, a file over HTTPS or SFTP, the Google Ads Data Manager, or the Google Ads API.
- Uploads must come within 90 days of the click. Reports show them after 24 to 48 hours.
- The click id is case-sensitive.

nodes.title: The click id can ride in links, with nothing stored in the browser
nodes.body:
**Your question:** can the click id ride in the link without storing anything in the browser?

**Short answer: yes, our inference from how links work.** A short script on www reads `gclid` from the address. It adds `?gclid=...` to the signup link, and to every link to another www page. Then the id survives a visit to the pricing page first. The script writes no cookie and no browser storage. If the visitor closes the tab, the id is gone.

**One catch: Umami stores the click id too.** Umami saves the full query string of every page view. It also saves `gclid` in a column of its own. So our anonymous www data would hold a per-click id.
- Fix: the tracker option `data-before-send` runs a function before each send. It can delete `gclid` from the address and keep the UTM tags.
- Do not use `data-exclude-search`. It drops the whole query string, so the UTM campaign reports go empty. This is our inference from Umami's code.

**A second catch: Google wants a consent signal.** Google's upload docs "highly recommend" a consent field, `ad_user_data`, on each conversion. Without it, conversions may not be attributable. Google does not say exactly what it does with EEA conversions that have no consent field. Not confirmed. "Do we ask new users before we send their click id to Google Ads?" asks what we do.

**Also:** Google now marks the file and Sheets upload as "legacy". The Google Ads API is the long-term path. Sheets still works today.

- https://docs.umami.is/docs/tracker-configuration

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Why Umami on Postgres could fail within a year, and the way out
nodes.body:
**The question:** assume "Umami runs both sites, on its own Postgres, apart from the app database" failed a year from now. Why? This whole node is our inference, based on the sources below.

**Strongest reasons it failed:**
1. **Reports got slow.** Umami on Postgres has known trouble with long date ranges. One user with about 12M page views and 2.6M events reported: 7 days fine, 30 days unreliable, all-time out of memory. At 2M app events per month we pass that in two months. Retention and funnel reports over a quarter would suffer first.
2. **The database grew without end.** Umami has no setting to delete old events. The maintainer says it is a job for a scheduled script. Without one, the database and its backup grow by about 24M rows a year.
3. **The fix ate the contractor's hours.** Umami can store events in ClickHouse, but this is not officially supported. Each Umami upgrade then needs hand-made schema changes. That does not fit 10 hours a month.
4. **The way out was slow.** PostHog cloud for the app is a new sub-processor. "Any new sub-processor means a DPA update and 30 days' notice to customers" applies, so the switch takes at least a month.
5. **Ad blockers hid app users.** Some block lists match Umami's script name. Umami lets us rename the script and its endpoint.

**Strongest alternative:** Umami for www, PostHog EU cloud for the app. But you already chose to revisit that only if Umami gets slow. So it is not a new choice now.

**What keeps the decision safe:**
- Cut app volume with a small event list. "Keep the list to 10 to 20 events and estimate their volume" does this.
- Delete old raw events on a schedule. "How long do we keep raw app events in Umami?" asks for how long.
- Rename the script and endpoint from day one.
- Watch report speed for 30 and 90 days after the first month. Slow reports start the 30-day notice for PostHog.

Sources:
- https://github.com/umami-software/umami/issues/1253
- https://github.com/umami-software/umami/issues/1277
- https://github.com/umami-software/umami/discussions/3389
- https://docs.umami.is/docs/bypass-ad-blockers

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: We accept that ad blockers hide some visitors; signup counts come from our database
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user** in "We'll live with it".

- Some visitors block the Umami script. Our www and app numbers will be lower than the truth. We accept this: marketing numbers are directional.
- **The true signup count comes from the app database,** not from Umami. Use Umami for trends and campaign shares, not for exact counts.
- **We build nothing against ad blockers:** no proxy, no events sent from our server.

**One free step stays, our recommendation:** give the script and its endpoint plain names from day one, as "Why Umami on Postgres could fail within a year, and the way out" says. That is two settings, `TRACKER_SCRIPT_NAME` and `COLLECT_API_ENDPOINT`, and no code. Some block lists match Umami's default names. Drop it if you prefer zero changes.

**For the side-by-side month:** Google Analytics is blocked too, often more. Compare signups with the app database, not GA with Umami.

Sources: https://docs.umami.is/docs/environment-variables, https://docs.umami.is/docs/bypass-ad-blockers

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Two readers, one shared Umami dashboard, no reports
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user** in "Me monthly, Jonas weekly".

- **You** (the founder) read the numbers once a month: signups, the funnel from `signed_up` to `review_link_sent`, and which firms use time tracking and invoices.
- **Jonas** (marketing) reads them once a week: www page views, referrers and UTM campaigns.
- **Form:** one shared Umami dashboard. No emailed reports, no data in a CRM, no extra tool.

What follows, our inference:
- Each of you gets your own Umami login. Nothing else is needed, so this adds no work and no cost.
- Billing questions still need a manual Stripe export, as "No billing events in Umami; plan rides on the account, billing stays in Stripe" says. A few times a quarter is fine.

This closes "Who reads the analytics, and in what form?": it adds nothing to the tool choice.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Decision record, draft 1: Umami on our Hetzner server, about 9 EUR a month
nodes.body:
**Your request:** the one-page decision record, with the monthly cost. Every line below comes from a settled node, named in brackets. Two items are still open; see the end.

**1. Tool.** Umami, for www and the app. [Umami runs both sites, on its own Postgres, apart from the app database]

**2. Hosting.** Our Hetzner servers in Germany, Docker Compose: the Umami container plus its own Postgres, apart from the app database. It goes into the contractor's existing backup job. [We self-host on Hetzner in Germany with Docker Compose, for 80 EUR/month or less]

**3. What we track.**
- www: anonymous page views, referrers and UTM campaigns. No cookies, no banner. [App events link to the logged-in account; www stays anonymous with no cookies]
- App: six events, user id and account id only, no page views. [The app event list is final: six events, and no page views inside the app]
- Raw app events stay 13 months, then only monthly totals. [Raw app events stay 13 months; older months survive only as monthly totals]
- Billing stays in Stripe. Ad blockers: accepted. [We accept that ad blockers hide some visitors; signup counts come from our database]

**4. Migration.**
1. Install Umami. Put the tracker on www and in the app.
2. Build the click id path: `gclid` in links, the unticked checkbox at signup, a daily upload to Google Ads as a secondary conversion. [New users tick an unticked checkbox at signup before their click id goes to Google Ads; no banner, ever]
3. Run GA and Umami side by side for one of Jonas's campaign months. [GA and Umami run side by side for one full campaign month, then GA goes]
4. Jonas exports 12 monthly totals. Make the upload primary. Remove GA.

**5. GDPR stance.** Self-hosted Umami adds no sub-processor. App analytics runs under the customer DPA. The privacy notice names the Google Ads upload, the checkbox and the 13 months. A lawyer confirms the checkbox wording. [Any new sub-processor means a DPA update and 30 days' notice to customers]

**6. Monthly cost** (excl. VAT):

| Item | Per month |
|---|---|
| Umami software (open source) | 0 EUR |
| Server: shared at first; own Hetzner CX33 (4 vCPU, 8 GB) when needed | 0 to 8.99 EUR |
| Backup, in the existing job | 0 EUR |
| Google Ads upload | 0 EUR |
| Contractor: upgrades, retention job, a speed check | about 1 to 2 of his 10 hours |
| **Total** | **about 9 EUR plus 1 to 2 hours; cap is 80 EUR** |

One-off setup, our estimate: about 10 to 15 contractor hours over the first two months. The hours are invented; only the server price is checked. Hetzner shows the CX33 as "not available" in some locations today; the CX23 (2 vCPU, 4 GB) at 5.99 EUR also fits 100k events, our inference.

**Fallback cost:** if 30- or 90-day reports get slow, the app moves to PostHog EU cloud. At 100k events this is in its free tier, but it adds a sub-processor and 30 days' notice. [Why Umami on Postgres could fail within a year, and the way out]

**Still open before this is final:**
- "What do we do when a user or a customer asks us to delete their analytics data?"
- "Pick the side-by-side month and who removes the GA script"
- Check that Hetzner is on our DPA sub-processor list.

Sources: https://www.hetzner.com/cloud/cost-optimized (checked 2026-11-17), https://docs.umami.is/docs/install, https://posthog.com/docs/product-analytics/pricing

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What do we do when a user or a customer asks us to delete their analytics data?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** App events carry the user id and the account id, under the customer DPA. Raw events stay 13 months. This is the last gap in the GDPR stance of "Decision record, draft 1: Umami on our Hetzner server, about 9 EUR a month".

**The problem:** two cases need deletion before the 13 months end.
- A user asks us to erase their data. GDPR gives us one month to act.
- A customer firm ends its contract. Most DPAs say we delete its data at the end.

Umami has no button for this, our inference from its database schema. The user id sits in the `distinct_id` column of the session tables. Events link to sessions, and nothing deletes them in cascade. So deletion means a small database script across several tables.

**What hangs on it:** the privacy notice and DPA text, one more job for the contractor, and whether the decision record can be final.

Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/umami-software/umami/master/prisma/schema.prisma; GDPR Article 12(3) and Article 17, https://gdpr-info.eu/art-12-gdpr/

options.label: Delete on request with one script (recommended)
options.detail: The contractor writes one script that deletes all Umami rows for a user id or an account id. He runs it on each request and when a customer leaves. Cost: about 2 hours once, minutes per request.

options.label: Wait for the 13-month expiry
options.detail: We do nothing per request; the monthly job removes the data within 13 months. Cost: no work, but it likely misses the one-month deadline for erasure. Our inference, not legal advice.

options.label: Send a random analytics id, not the real ids
options.detail: The app sends a random id per user and per account, and keeps the mapping in the app database. Deleting the user in the app cuts the link. Cost: app changes, and a lawyer must agree the left-over rows are no longer personal.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Pick the side-by-side month and who removes the GA script
nodes.body:
**What is needed:** two facts for step 3 and 4 of the migration in "Decision record, draft 1: Umami on our Hetzner server, about 9 EUR a month".

1. **Which month.** Ask Jonas which campaign month fits. Umami and the Google Ads upload must both be live before it starts, as "GA and Umami run side by side for one full campaign month, then GA goes" says. So the month must start at least as far ahead as the setup takes, about two months by our estimate.
2. **Who removes the GA script, and when.** One name and one date, the first working day after Jonas's export. The same person switches the Google Ads upload from secondary to primary on that day.

Reply with a comment that holds the month and the name.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Decide how a small SaaS replaces Google Analytics with a self-hosted, privacy-friendly setup
nodes.body:
## Destination
A one-page decision record. It states which tool we use, where it runs, what we track, how we migrate, and what it costs per month.

## Notes
- **SaaS**: our B2B web app (app.example.com) plus our marketing site (www.example.com).
- **Product analytics**: in-app events, such as signup and feature use. This is different from marketing page views.
- **Marketing analytics**: page views, referrers and campaigns on the marketing site.
- Standing preferences: low ops burden. EU customers matter. Avoid cookie banners if possible.

## Done when
- The tool is chosen.
- The hosting is chosen.
- The event list is agreed.
- The migration steps are written.
- The monthly cost is estimated.
- The GDPR stance is stated.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Do we use one tool for both sites, or one tool for each?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** Today Google Analytics (GA) covers the marketing site and maybe the app. We want to replace it with a self-hosted, privacy-friendly setup.

**The problem:** The two sites need different things. The marketing site needs page views, referrers and campaigns. The app needs events per user, such as signup and feature use, and funnels. Some tools do both. Some tools do only one job well.

**What hangs on it:** The tool choice, the hosting, the cost, and the ops burden. Two tools double the work to run them.

options.label: One tool for both sites (recommended)
options.detail: One install covers page views on www and events in the app. Cost: the tool must be good at both jobs, so fewer tools qualify.

options.label: Two tools, one per job
options.detail: A light page-view tool runs on www. A product analytics tool runs in the app. Cost: two installs to run, two bills, and two places to look.

options.label: Product analytics only
options.detail: We track the app well and keep only simple counts on www, for example from server logs. Cost: we lose campaign and referrer reports for marketing.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Who runs the analytics servers?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** The goal says "self-hosted". The standing preferences also say low ops burden and EU customers matter.

**The problem:** These pull in different directions. Running the tool ourselves gives full control of the data. It also adds upgrades, backups and monitoring. Many open-source tools also sell a managed cloud in the EU. That keeps the data in the EU with little ops work, but the vendor holds the data.

**What hangs on it:** The monthly cost, the ops tasks we must plan, and part of the GDPR stance.

options.label: The tool vendor runs it in the EU (recommended)
options.detail: We use the managed cloud of an open-source tool, with an EU data region. Cost: a monthly fee, and the data is on the vendor's servers, not ours.

options.label: We run it on a small EU server
options.detail: We install the open-source tool on one rented server in the EU. Cost: we do upgrades, backups and monitoring ourselves.

options.label: We run it on our existing app infrastructure
options.detail: The tool runs next to the app, in our current cloud account. Cost: analytics load can affect the app, and the same team carries it.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: In the app, do we track named users or only anonymous counts?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** We want to avoid cookie banners. We also want product analytics in the app, such as signup and feature use.

**The problem:** Anonymous page counts without cookies usually need no banner. Linking events to a logged-in user is personal data. It needs a legal basis, for example our contract with the customer or legitimate interest. Example: "account Acme used the export feature 12 times this week" is personal data. "The export feature was used 340 times" is not.

**What hangs on it:** Which tools qualify, the event list, whether we need a banner, and the GDPR stance.

options.label: Named users in the app, anonymous on www (recommended)
options.detail: The app links events to the logged-in account. The marketing site uses no cookies and no personal data. Cost: the app privacy notice must cover analytics, and the tool must store user ids.

options.label: Anonymous everywhere
options.detail: No user ids on either site. No banner anywhere. Cost: no per-user or per-account funnels, so questions such as 'which accounts use feature X' stay open.

options.label: Named users everywhere, with a banner
options.detail: Both sites set cookies and link visits to people. Cost: a cookie banner on www, which we want to avoid, and less data from people who decline.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What do we do with our historical Google Analytics data?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** We will remove Google Analytics (GA). GA holds our past traffic data.

**The problem:** The new tool counts differently. Most old data cannot move over cleanly. We must decide what, if anything, we keep.

**What hangs on it:** The migration steps, and whether we run GA and the new tool side by side for a while.

options.label: Export key reports, then drop GA (recommended)
options.detail: We save a few monthly summaries, such as visits per page and per source, as files. Cost: we cannot query the old raw data later.

options.label: Import history into the new tool
options.detail: We load old GA data into the new tool, so charts run back in time. Cost: few tools support this well, and the numbers do not match one to one.

options.label: Start fresh, keep nothing
options.detail: We remove GA and start from zero. Cost: no year-over-year comparison for the first year.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: List what we use Google Analytics for today
nodes.body:
Write down every report, dashboard, alert and integration that uses Google Analytics (GA) today, and who uses it. Include links to Google Ads or other tools, for example conversion tracking.

This tells us what the new setup must replace, and what we can drop. The tool choice and the migration steps depend on it.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Measure our monthly traffic and event volume
nodes.body:
Find the numbers for one normal month:
- page views on the marketing site
- page views and active users in the app
- an estimate of in-app events, for example signups and feature use

Most analytics tools price by monthly events or page views. Server size also depends on volume. The monthly cost estimate cannot start without these numbers.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Draft the first event list for the app
nodes.body:
Write a short list of in-app events, for example: signed up, invited a teammate, created first project, used feature X, upgraded plan. For each event, write the question it answers and the properties it carries.

Keep it small: 10 to 20 events. Mark any property that is personal data. The answer to "In the app, do we track named users or only anonymous counts?" decides which properties are allowed.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Candidate tools fall into two groups
nodes.body:
This is my inference from general knowledge, not yet checked against current vendor pages.

- **Page-view tools**: Plausible, Umami, Matomo. They count visits without cookies. They are light to run. Matomo also has some event and user features.
- **Product analytics tools**: PostHog. It tracks events per user, funnels and retention. It is much heavier to self-host.

Plausible, Umami, Matomo and PostHog all have an open-source version and a managed cloud. Check the prices and EU regions before a choice.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What GDPR documents and steps do we need?
nodes.body: The GDPR stance must be stated. The exact parts are not clear yet. Likely areas: a data processing agreement with any vendor, the privacy notice text, how long we keep data, and how we handle a request to delete a user's data. The answers to the hosting and named-user questions shape this.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What breaks when ad blockers block the tracker?
nodes.body: Many ad blockers block analytics scripts, also privacy-friendly ones. Our numbers could be low, mostly among technical B2B users. Options may include a proxy on our own domain, or sending app events from the server. The size of the problem and the fix are not clear yet.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: How do we run the cut-over from Google Analytics?
nodes.body: The migration order is not clear yet. Open points: do we run both tools side by side, for how long, how we check that the numbers agree, and when we remove the GA script and any cookie banner.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Who reads the analytics, and in what form?
nodes.body: We do not know yet who looks at the numbers: founders, marketing, product, sales. Each group may need different views, such as a weekly email, a shared dashboard, or account data in the CRM. This may add needs to the tool choice.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Named users in the app, anonymous on www (recommended)
nodes.body: Yes. Customers already sign a DPA with us, analytics in the app goes under that. Marketing site stays anonymous, no banner. I hate cookie banners.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: We run it ourselves on Hetzner (Germany), Docker Compose, same as everything else. No Kubernetes. Our DevOps contractor has ~10h/month, so it has to be boring to run.
nodes.body: Not against an EU cloud plan if it's clearly cheaper than his hours. Budget is ~80 EUR/month max. We already run Postgres there, if the tool can use it, even better.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Export key reports, then drop GA (recommended)
nodes.body: Jonas (marketing) wants the last 12 months of monthly totals. Nobody needs raw data.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: Ballpark: 40k pageviews, ~2M app events/month
nodes.body:
Rough numbers:
- marketing site: ~40k pageviews/month
- app: ~1,800 weekly active users
- if we track features properly, maybe 2M events/month. That is a guess.

nodes.author: user
nodes.title: GA today: page views, UTM campaigns, signup hack
nodes.body:
Honestly not much:
- marketing page views + UTM campaign tracking. Jonas cares about this one.
- a few hacked signup "events".
Nobody looks at the GA funnels. No Google Ads conversion stuff I know of, will ask Jonas.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: App events link to the logged-in account; www stays anonymous with no cookies
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user** in reply to "In the app, do we track named users or only anonymous counts?".

- **App (app.example.com):** events link to the logged-in user and account. The legal basis is the data processing agreement (DPA) that each customer already signs with us. Analytics in the app goes under that DPA.
- **Marketing site (www.example.com):** anonymous counts only. No cookies, no personal data, no cookie banner.

What follows from this (my inference):
- The tool must support an "identify" call for the app, and a cookieless mode for www.
- If a vendor cloud stores app events, that vendor becomes a sub-processor. Our customer DPA must then list it.
- "Draft the first event list for the app" can now start: user id and account id are allowed properties in the app.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: We self-host on Hetzner in Germany with Docker Compose, for 80 EUR/month or less
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user** in reply to "Who runs the analytics servers?".

- **Where:** our own Hetzner servers in Germany, next to what we already run.
- **How:** Docker Compose. No Kubernetes.
- **Ops budget:** our DevOps contractor has about 10 hours per month in total. The tool must be boring to run: few moving parts, easy upgrades.
- **Money budget:** 80 EUR per month at most.
- **Exception:** an EU managed cloud is allowed if it is clearly cheaper than the contractor's hours.
- **Bonus:** we already run Postgres there. A tool that can use it is preferred.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Keep 12 months of monthly totals as files, then remove Google Analytics
nodes.body:
**Decided by the user** in reply to "What do we do with our historical Google Analytics data?".

- Jonas (marketing) gets the last 12 months of monthly totals, exported from Google Analytics (GA) as files.
- Nobody needs the raw data. We do not import history into the new tool.
- After the export, we remove GA.

So GA import support does not count when we compare tools.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Planning volume: about 40k page views and 2M app events per month
nodes.body:
Source: the user's estimate in "Ballpark: 40k pageviews, ~2M app events/month". The app event number is a guess.

| Site | Volume per month |
|---|---|
| www.example.com | about 40,000 page views |
| app.example.com | about 1,800 weekly active users, about 2,000,000 events |

What this means (my inference, prices from "Tool facts checked against vendor pages"):
- 40k page views is small. Every candidate tool handles it, and some free cloud tiers cover it.
- 2M events is about 1,100 events per active user per month, or about 50 per user per working day. That is a lot for a first event list of 10 to 20 events. The real number is likely lower.
- The app number decides the cost. It also rules out PostHog self-hosted, which its vendor says struggles above about 300k events per month.
- We can use these numbers for the cost estimate now. We check them after one month on the new tool.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: The new setup must replace page views, UTM campaigns and signup events
nodes.body:
Source: the user's list in "GA today: page views, UTM campaigns, signup hack".

**Must replace:**
- Page views on the marketing site.
- UTM campaign tracking. A UTM tag is a set of parameters in a link, such as `?utm_source=newsletter`, that says where a visitor came from. Jonas (marketing) uses this.
- Signup events. Today these are hacked into GA. In the new setup they become real events in "Draft the first event list for the app".

**Can drop:** GA funnels. Nobody looks at them.

**Not known yet:** Google Ads conversion tracking. The user will ask Jonas. If Google Ads needs conversions, we need a plan for it, because the Ads tag sets its own cookies.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Ask Jonas about Google Ads and the 12 monthly totals he wants
nodes.body:
Before we remove Google Analytics (GA), ask Jonas (marketing) two things:

1. **Google Ads:** do we send conversions from GA to Google Ads, or run any Ads campaign that depends on GA? If yes, removing GA breaks it.
2. **Monthly totals:** which totals does he want for the last 12 months? For example: page views per page, visits per source, visits per UTM campaign, signups per month.

Write his answers as an answer to this task. Answer 1 can change the tool choice. Answer 2 sets the export step in the cut-over.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What the four candidate tools need and do, from their own pages
nodes.body:
**Why this node exists:** "Candidate tools fall into two groups" named four tools: Umami, Plausible, Matomo and PostHog. This node checks each one against the vendor's own pages. It tests them against our limits: Hetzner, Docker Compose, 80 EUR/month or less, and a contractor with about 10 hours per month.

**Terms used below:**
- *Identify*: link events to the logged-in account.
- *Funnel*: the share of users who go through steps in order, for example signup, then first project.
- *Retention*: the share of users who come back in later weeks.
- *ClickHouse*: a second database type that some tools need. It is one more service to run and back up.

**Umami**
- To run it: one container and a Postgres database. Docker Compose works.
- www without cookies: yes.
- App: identify, funnels and retention, all three.
- Cloud price: free up to 100k events/month for 1 site; Pro is $20/month.

**Plausible Community Edition (self-hosted)**
- To run it: Postgres plus ClickHouse, Docker Compose, 2 GB RAM.
- www without cookies: yes.
- App: custom events only. No identify, no retention, no funnels in the self-hosted edition.
- Cloud price: $19 to $39/month at 100k page views. No free tier.

**Matomo**
- To run it: PHP and MySQL or MariaDB. It does not support Postgres.
- www without cookies: possible. But Matomo says that in Germany, only its server-log mode is clearly free of consent.
- App: User ID, yes. Funnels: the pages did not say; it may be a paid plugin.
- Cloud price: Frankfurt hosting, €29/month for 50k hits.

**PostHog**
- To run it: Postgres, ClickHouse, Kafka, Redis, Zookeeper and MinIO, on 4 vCPU and 16 GB. The vendor gives no support for this. It warns it may struggle above about 300k events/month.
- www without cookies: yes, in its cookieless mode.
- App: identify, funnels and retention. Its reports are the deepest of the four.
- Cloud price: Frankfurt hosting. The first 1M events per month are free, then about $0.00005 per event. At 2M events that is about $50/month. Identified events can cost more.

**What this changes:**
- Umami is more than a page-view counter. It covers the app too.
- PostHog self-hosted does not fit our ops budget. Only its cloud is a real option.
- Matomo adds a MySQL database next to our Postgres.

**Hosting cost:** a Hetzner 4 vCPU / 8 GB shared server (CX33) is about €8.99/month. The page showed some plans as "currently unavailable", so check before you order.

All prices exclude VAT. Checked on 2026-11-17.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Which tool do we run for the app and the marketing site?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** We self-host on Hetzner with Docker Compose, for 80 EUR/month or less, and the contractor has about 10 hours per month. The app tracks named users; www stays anonymous with no cookies. "Tool facts checked against vendor pages" lists what each tool needs.

**The problem:** No tool is best at every part. Umami fits the hosting best: it uses our Postgres and does both jobs. PostHog has the deepest product analytics, but only its cloud fits our ops budget. Matomo is left out: it cannot use Postgres and adds MySQL. PostHog self-hosted is left out: it needs six services and struggles at our volume.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Umami and PostHog both record sessions and can hide all text on screen
nodes.body:
**Your question:** can any candidate tool record app sessions (session replay) and hide our customers' project data?

**Short answer:** yes. Umami, our chosen tool, can do it on our own server. So the recordings never leave Hetzner.

**Umami** (since version 3.1.0, self-hosted too):
- You switch it on per website, in the admin page "Replays & Heatmaps". A second small script loads next to the tracker.
- Default mode hides all input fields. A strict mode hides all inputs and all text on the page. You can also hide chosen page parts with CSS selectors.
- It records 15% of sessions by default; you can set 0% to 100%.
- A recording stops after 5 minutes by default. Umami keeps recordings for 30 days; you can save the ones you want.

**PostHog** (cloud only for us, see "Umami runs both sites, on its own Postgres, apart from the app database"):
- It hides input fields by default, but not other text.
- To hide all text, set `maskTextSelector: "*"`. To blank a whole area, add the class `ph-no-capture`.

**Plausible:** no session replay. **Matomo:** only through a paid plugin; not checked further, because Matomo is out.

**Risks, our inference:**
- Strict mode hides text, but it does not hide images, canvas drawings or plans. Architects' drawings may still show. Test on a real project screen before you switch it on.
- Recordings tie to named users in the app. Our privacy notice and customer contract must then say we record sessions.
- Recordings add data to the Umami Postgres. A low sample rate keeps this small.

**If you want it later:** strict mode, a low sample rate (for example 5%), and a test on real screens first. It needs no new tool.

Sources:
- https://docs.umami.is/docs, https://docs.umami.is/docs/replays
- https://posthog.com/docs/session-replay/privacy

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Google Ads takes signups from our server if we keep the ad click id
nodes.body:
**Why this matters:** Jonas's Google Ads campaigns need signup conversions. Today they come from Google Analytics, which we remove.

**How Google Ads takes conversions without its script** (Google's "offline conversion import"):
- Google adds a click id, `gclid`, to the landing page address when someone clicks an ad. This needs auto-tagging on in the Ads account.
- We keep that id with the new account. Later we upload rows of "click id, conversion name, time".
- Upload ways: Google Sheets with a scheduled import, a file over HTTPS or SFTP, the Google Ads Data Manager, or the Google Ads API.
- Uploads must come within 90 days of the click. Reports show them after 24 to 48 hours.
- The click id is case-sensitive.

**The second way, "enhanced conversions for leads":** we upload a SHA256 hash of the signup email. Google matches it to signed-in Google users who clicked an ad. Google's page says it also matches to data from the website form, so it may need a Google script on the signup page. Not confirmed.

**Conflict with our rules, our inference:** Google's own guide stores the click id in a cookie or browser storage on every page. That breaks "App events link to the logged-in account; www stays anonymous with no cookies". A way around it: www reads the click id from the address and adds it to the signup link. Nothing is stored in the browser. We lose a conversion when a visitor leaves and comes back later.

**Legal point, our inference:** sending a named customer's click id or email hash to Google is a transfer of personal data. It needs a legal basis and a line in the privacy notice. It belongs to "What GDPR documents and steps do we need?".

Sources:
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7014069
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7012522

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: How do we send signup conversions to Google Ads without Google Analytics?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** Jonas spends about €1.5k/month on Google Ads. Ads gets signup conversions from Google Analytics today, and we remove Google Analytics. Jonas accepts another path if it is little work. "Google Ads takes signups from our server if we keep the ad click id" lists the ways.

**The problem:** Every way costs either privacy or accuracy. Google's usual setup stores the click id in the browser on every page. Our rule says www stores nothing. Example: a visitor clicks an ad, reads the pricing page, and signs up the same day. The click id can ride along in the links. If he comes back a week later from a bookmark, the id is gone and that signup is not counted.

**What hangs on it:** the work for the app team, whether a consent banner returns on www, the GDPR steps for data sent to Google, and the day we can remove Google Analytics.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: The click id can ride in links, with nothing stored in the browser
nodes.body:
**Your question:** can the click id ride in the link without storing anything in the browser?

**Short answer: yes, our inference from how links work.** A short script on www reads `gclid` from the address. It adds `?gclid=...` to the signup link, and to every link to another www page. Then the id survives a visit to the pricing page first. The script writes no cookie and no browser storage. If the visitor closes the tab, the id is gone.

**One catch: Umami stores the click id too.** Umami saves the full query string of every page view. It also saves `gclid` in a column of its own. So our anonymous www data would hold a per-click id.
- Fix: the tracker option `data-before-send` runs a function before each send. It can delete `gclid` from the address and keep the UTM tags.
- Do not use `data-exclude-search`. It drops the whole query string, so the UTM campaign reports go empty. This is our inference from Umami's code.

**A second catch: Google wants a consent signal.** Google's upload docs "highly recommend" a consent field, `ad_user_data`, on each conversion. Without it, conversions may not be attributable. Google does not say exactly what it does with EEA conversions that have no consent field. Not confirmed. "Do we ask new users before we send their click id to Google Ads?" asks what we do.

**Also:** Google now marks the file and Sheets upload as "legacy". The Google Ads API is the long-term path. Sheets still works today.

Sources:
- https://docs.umami.is/docs/tracker-configuration
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/umami-software/umami/master/prisma/schema.prisma
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/umami-software/umami/master/src/app/api/send/route.ts
- https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/docs/conversions/upload-clicks
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7014069

**The problem:** The click id of a named new customer is personal data. Sending it to Google needs a legal basis. Google also asks for a consent signal, `ad_user_data`, on each upload from the EU. Without it, Google says conversions may not be attributable. The signup form is the one place where we can ask, because the visitor is already in the app.

**What hangs on it:** the signup form, the privacy notice text, the columns in the daily upload, and how many signups Jonas's campaigns see.

Source: https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/docs/conversions/upload-clicks

options.detail: We name the upload in the privacy notice and send no consent field. Cost: no extra work, but Google may not attribute these conversions, and the legal basis is weaker.

nodes.title: Any new sub-processor means a DPA update and 30 days' notice to customers
nodes.body:
**Stated by the user** in "DPA lists sub-processors: update it, notify customers 30 days ahead".

- A new one means: update the list, and tell customers 30 days before it starts.

**What this means for the choices so far, our inference:**
- Self-hosted Umami on our Hetzner servers adds no sub-processor. Umami is software we run, not a vendor. This holds if Hetzner is already on the list. Check that it is.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Why Umami on Postgres could fail within a year, and the way out
nodes.body:
**The question:** assume "Umami runs both sites, on its own Postgres, apart from the app database" failed a year from now. Why? This whole node is our inference, based on the sources below.

**Strongest reasons it failed:**
1. **Reports got slow.** Umami on Postgres has known trouble with long date ranges. One user with about 12M page views and 2.6M events reported: 7 days fine, 30 days unreliable, all-time out of memory. At 2M app events per month we pass that in two months. Retention and funnel reports over a quarter would suffer first.
2. **The database grew without end.** Umami has no setting to delete old events. The maintainer says it is a job for a scheduled script. Without one, the database and its backup grow by about 24M rows a year.
3. **The fix ate the contractor's hours.** Umami can store events in ClickHouse, but this is not officially supported. Each Umami upgrade then needs hand-made schema changes. That does not fit 10 hours a month.
4. **The way out was slow.** PostHog cloud for the app is a new sub-processor. "Any new sub-processor means a DPA update and 30 days' notice to customers" applies, so the switch takes at least a month.
5. **Ad blockers hid app users.** Some block lists match Umami's script name. Umami lets us rename the script and its endpoint.

**Strongest alternative:** Umami for www, PostHog EU cloud for the app. But you already chose to revisit that only if Umami gets slow. So it is not a new choice now.

**What keeps the decision safe:**
- Cut app volume with a small event list. "Keep the list to 10 to 20 events and estimate their volume" does this.
- Delete old raw events on a schedule. "How long do we keep raw app events in Umami?" asks for how long.
- Rename the script and endpoint from day one.
- Watch report speed for 30 and 90 days after the first month. Slow reports start the 30-day notice for PostHog.

Sources:
- https://github.com/umami-software/umami/issues/1253
- https://github.com/umami-software/umami/issues/1277
- https://github.com/umami-software/umami/discussions/3389
- https://docs.umami.is/docs/bypass-ad-blockers

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Decide how a small SaaS replaces Google Analytics with a self-hosted, privacy-friendly setup
nodes.body:
## Destination
A one-page decision record. It states which tool we use, where it runs, what we track, how we migrate, and what it costs per month.

## Notes
- **SaaS**: our B2B web app (app.example.com) plus our marketing site (www.example.com).
- **Product analytics**: in-app events, such as signup and feature use. This is different from marketing page views.
- **Marketing analytics**: page views, referrers and campaigns on the marketing site.
- Standing preferences: low ops burden. EU customers matter. Avoid cookie banners if possible.

## Done when
- The tool is chosen.
- The hosting is chosen.
- The event list is agreed.
- The migration steps are written.
- The monthly cost is estimated.
- The GDPR stance is stated.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Do we use one tool for both sites, or one tool for each?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** Today Google Analytics (GA) covers the marketing site and maybe the app. We want to replace it with a self-hosted, privacy-friendly setup.

**The problem:** The two sites need different things. The marketing site needs page views, referrers and campaigns. The app needs events per user, such as signup and feature use, and funnels. Some tools do both. Some tools do only one job well.

**What hangs on it:** The tool choice, the hosting, the cost, and the ops burden. Two tools double the work to run them.

options.label: One tool for both sites (recommended)
options.detail: One install covers page views on www and events in the app. Cost: the tool must be good at both jobs, so fewer tools qualify.

options.label: Two tools, one per job
options.detail: A light page-view tool runs on www. A product analytics tool runs in the app. Cost: two installs to run, two bills, and two places to look.

options.label: Product analytics only
options.detail: We track the app well and keep only simple counts on www, for example from server logs. Cost: we lose campaign and referrer reports for marketing.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Who runs the analytics servers?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** The goal says "self-hosted". The standing preferences also say low ops burden and EU customers matter.

**The problem:** These pull in different directions. Running the tool ourselves gives full control of the data. It also adds upgrades, backups and monitoring. Many open-source tools also sell a managed cloud in the EU. That keeps the data in the EU with little ops work, but the vendor holds the data.

**What hangs on it:** The monthly cost, the ops tasks we must plan, and part of the GDPR stance.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: What the four candidate tools need and do, from their own pages
nodes.body:
**Why this node exists:** "Candidate tools fall into two groups" named four tools: Umami, Plausible, Matomo and PostHog. This node checks each one against the vendor's own pages. It tests them against our limits: Hetzner, Docker Compose, 80 EUR/month or less, and a contractor with about 10 hours per month.

**Terms used below:**
- *Identify*: link events to the logged-in account.
- *Funnel*: the share of users who go through steps in order, for example signup, then first project.
- *Retention*: the share of users who come back in later weeks.
- *ClickHouse*: a second database type that some tools need. It is one more service to run and back up.

**Umami**
- To run it: one container and a Postgres database. Docker Compose works.
- www without cookies: yes.
- App: identify, funnels and retention, all three.
- Cloud price: free up to 100k events/month for 1 site; Pro is $20/month.

**Plausible Community Edition (self-hosted)**
- To run it: Postgres plus ClickHouse, Docker Compose, 2 GB RAM.
- www without cookies: yes.
- App: custom events only. No identify, no retention, no funnels in the self-hosted edition.
- Cloud price: $19 to $39/month at 100k page views. No free tier.

**Matomo**
- To run it: PHP and MySQL or MariaDB. It does not support Postgres.
- www without cookies: possible. But Matomo says that in Germany, only its server-log mode is clearly free of consent.
- App: User ID, yes. Funnels: the pages did not say; it may be a paid plugin.
- Cloud price: Frankfurt hosting, €29/month for 50k hits.

**PostHog**
- To run it: Postgres, ClickHouse, Kafka, Redis, Zookeeper and MinIO, on 4 vCPU and 16 GB. The vendor gives no support for this. It warns it may struggle above about 300k events/month.
- www without cookies: yes, in its cookieless mode.
- App: identify, funnels and retention. Its reports are the deepest of the four.
- Cloud price: Frankfurt hosting. The first 1M events per month are free, then about $0.00005 per event. At 2M events that is about $50/month. Identified events can cost more.

**What this changes:**
- Umami is more than a page-view counter. It covers the app too.
- PostHog self-hosted does not fit our ops budget. Only its cloud is a real option.
- Matomo adds a MySQL database next to our Postgres.

**Hosting cost:** a Hetzner 4 vCPU / 8 GB shared server (CX33) is about €8.99/month. The page showed some plans as "currently unavailable", so check before you order.

All prices exclude VAT. Checked on 2026-11-17.

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Umami and PostHog both record sessions and can hide all text on screen
nodes.body:
**Your question:** can any candidate tool record app sessions (session replay) and hide our customers' project data?

**Short answer:** yes. Umami, our chosen tool, can do it on our own server. So the recordings never leave Hetzner.

**Umami** (since version 3.1.0, self-hosted too):
- You switch it on per website, in the admin page "Replays & Heatmaps". A second small script loads next to the tracker.
- Default mode hides all input fields. A strict mode hides all inputs and all text on the page. You can also hide chosen page parts with CSS selectors.
- It records 15% of sessions by default; you can set 0% to 100%.
- A recording stops after 5 minutes by default. Umami keeps recordings for 30 days; you can save the ones you want.

**PostHog** (cloud only for us, see "Umami runs both sites, on its own Postgres, apart from the app database"):
- It hides input fields by default, but not other text.
- To hide all text, set `maskTextSelector: "*"`. To blank a whole area, add the class `ph-no-capture`.

**Plausible:** no session replay. **Matomo:** only through a paid plugin; not checked further, because Matomo is out.

**Risks, our inference:**
- Strict mode hides text, but it does not hide images, canvas drawings or plans. Architects' drawings may still show. Test on a real project screen before you switch it on.
- Recordings tie to named users in the app. Our privacy notice and customer contract must then say we record sessions.
- Recordings add data to the Umami Postgres. A low sample rate keeps this small.

**If you want it later:** strict mode, a low sample rate (for example 5%), and a test on real screens first. It needs no new tool.

Sources:
- https://docs.umami.is/docs, https://docs.umami.is/docs/replays
- https://posthog.com/docs/session-replay/privacy

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: Google Ads takes signups from our server if we keep the ad click id
nodes.body:
**Why this matters:** Jonas's Google Ads campaigns need signup conversions. Today they come from Google Analytics, which we remove.

**How Google Ads takes conversions without its script** (Google's "offline conversion import"):
- Google adds a click id, `gclid`, to the landing page address when someone clicks an ad. This needs auto-tagging on in the Ads account.
- We keep that id with the new account. Later we upload rows of "click id, conversion name, time".
- Upload ways: Google Sheets with a scheduled import, a file over HTTPS or SFTP, the Google Ads Data Manager, or the Google Ads API.
- Uploads must come within 90 days of the click. Reports show them after 24 to 48 hours.
- The click id is case-sensitive.

**The second way, "enhanced conversions for leads":** we upload a SHA256 hash of the signup email. Google matches it to signed-in Google users who clicked an ad. Google's page says it also matches to data from the website form, so it may need a Google script on the signup page. Not confirmed.

**Conflict with our rules, our inference:** Google's own guide stores the click id in a cookie or browser storage on every page. That breaks "App events link to the logged-in account; www stays anonymous with no cookies". A way around it: www reads the click id from the address and adds it to the signup link. Nothing is stored in the browser. We lose a conversion when a visitor leaves and comes back later.

**Legal point, our inference:** sending a named customer's click id or email hash to Google is a transfer of personal data. It needs a legal basis and a line in the privacy notice. It belongs to "What GDPR documents and steps do we need?".

Sources:
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7014069
- https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7012522

nodes.author: agent
nodes.title: How do we send signup conversions to Google Ads without Google Analytics?
nodes.body:
**Where we are:** Jonas spends about €1.5k/month on Google Ads. Ads gets signup conversions from Google Analytics today, and we remove Google Analytics. Jonas accepts another path if it is little work. "Google Ads takes signups from our server if we keep the ad click id" lists the ways.

**The problem:** Every way costs either privacy or accuracy. Google's usual setup stores the click id in the browser on every page. Our rule says www stores nothing. Example: a visitor clicks an ad, reads the pricing page, and signs up the same day. The click id can ride along in the links. If he comes back a week later from a bookmark, the id is gone and that signup is not counted.

**What hangs on it:** the work for the app team, whether a consent banner returns on www, the GDPR steps for data sent to Google, and the day we can remove Google Analytics.

options.label: Pass the click id to signup, upload daily from our server (recommended)
options.detail: www adds the gclid from the address to the signup link. The app stores it with the account. A small daily job uploads new signups to a Google Sheet that Ads imports on a schedule. Cost: about a day of developer work, and we lose visitors who come back later without the id.

options.label: Upload a hash of the signup email
